title: Stoichiometry
description: Chemical equations, formulas from composition, amounts in reactions, limiting reagents and the concentrations of solutions.
overview: A balanced equation is a recipe: it says how many moles of each reactant combine, and how many moles of each product result. Stoichiometry is the arithmetic of that recipe. It tells a chemist how much starting material to weigh, how much product to expect, and how to measure an unknown by reacting it with a known.

This chapter balances equations, finds formulas from composition data, converts between amounts of reactants and products, identifies the limiting reagent, and then turns to solutions, where amounts are measured as concentrations and volumes.
objectives: Determine empirical and molecular formulas from percent composition or combustion analysis.
Carry out mass-to-mass calculations with mole ratios.
Find the limiting reagent, theoretical yield and percent yield.
Calculate and interconvert molarity, molality, mole fraction and mass percent, and do dilution calculations.
Analyze a titration to find an unknown concentration.

sections.title: Chemical equations and balancing
body: A **chemical equation** shows the **reactants** on the left and the **products** on the right, separated by an arrow, with phase labels (s), (l), (g) and (aq) for solid, liquid, gas and aqueous solution. Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction, a statement of the **conservation of mass** first established by Lavoisier. A **balanced equation** therefore has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. The numbers in front of formulas are the **coefficients**.

list: Write correct formulas for all species. Never change a subscript to balance an equation, since that changes the substance.
Balance elements that appear in only one reactant and one product first, then those that appear in several. Leave free elements (O₂, H₂) for last.
Use fractional coefficients if convenient, then multiply through to clear them.
Check that each element, and the total charge, balances.

example.title: Balancing propane combustion
solution: Carbon: 3 C on the left, so 3 CO₂. Hydrogen: 8 H on the left, so 4 H₂O. Oxygen on the right: 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 O atoms, so 5 O₂ on the left.

example.title: Balancing a redox reaction
solution: Iron: two Fe on the left, so 2 Fe. Oxygen: 3 from Fe₂O₃ and the CO must give 3 CO₂ (each CO₂ has two O, one from CO), so 3 CO and 3 CO₂ balance both C and O.

body: The coefficients give the ratio of moles, not of masses. In the propane reaction, 1 mol of C₃H₈ (44 g) consumes 5 mol of O₂ (160 g).

check.q: What is the coefficient of O₂ when C₄H₁₀ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers?
Why can’t you balance an equation by changing subscripts?
check.a: That would change which substance is present
wrong: Coefficients and subscripts mean the same thing
Subscripts are fixed by the periodic table

sections.title: Composition and formulas
body: The **percent composition** of a compound is the mass percent of each element: for a formula, (mass of element in one mole ÷ molar mass) × 100. For CaCO₃, carbon is 12.01/100.09 = 12.0% by mass.

Experiments often run in reverse, finding a formula from composition. The **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. To find it, convert each mass to moles, divide by the smallest, and, if the ratios are not whole numbers, multiply by a small integer. The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, found by dividing the experimental molar mass by the empirical formula mass.

example.title: From percent composition
example.problem: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.71% H and 53.3% O by mass, with molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹. Find its molecular formula.
solution: In 100 g: C 40.0/12.01 = 3.33 mol; H 6.71/1.008 = 6.66 mol; O 53.3/16.00 = 3.33 mol. Dividing by 3.33: C 1, H 2, O 1. The empirical formula is CH₂O, mass 30.03 g mol⁻¹.
180/30.03 = 6, so the molecular formula is **C₆H₁₂O₆** (glucose, for example).

body: For compounds of C, H and O, burn a weighed sample in excess O₂ and collect the CO₂ and H₂O. All the carbon is in the CO₂ and all the hydrogen in the H₂O. Oxygen is found by difference.

example.title: Combustion analysis
example.problem: Burning 0.5000 g of a compound containing only C, H and O gives 0.9553 g CO₂ and 0.5866 g H₂O. Find the empirical formula.
solution: Ratios C : H : O = 0.02171 : 0.06512 : 0.01086 = 2 : 6 : 1. The empirical formula is C₂H₆O (ethanol or dimethyl ether).

check.q: A compound has empirical formula CH₂ and molar mass 56 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?
In combustion analysis, where does all the hydrogen in the sample end up?

sections.title: Reaction stoichiometry
body: The coefficients of a balanced equation give the **mole ratio** between any two species. Every stoichiometry problem follows the same path:

body.eq: mass of A → moles of A → moles of B → mass of B

body: The first step uses the molar mass of A, the middle step the mole ratio from the equation, and the last step the molar mass of B. Calculations with gases or solutions replace the first and last steps with PV = nRT or with concentration and volume.

example.title: Mass to mass
example.problem: How many grams of CO₂ are produced by burning 25.0 g of propane, C₃H₈?

solution.eq: 25.0 g C₃H₈ × (1 mol / 44.10 g) × (3 mol CO₂ / 1 mol C₃H₈) × (44.01 g / 1 mol) = 74.8 g CO₂

body.key: Never compare grams of different substances. Convert to moles first.

check.q: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. How many moles of H₂O form from 3.0 mol of O₂ with excess H₂?
How many grams of NH₃ form from 6.00 g of H₂, with excess N₂? (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃)
check.why: 6.00 g H₂ = 2.98 mol, which gives 1.98 mol NH₃, or 33.8 g.

sections.title: Limiting reagent and yield
body: Reactants are rarely mixed in the exact ratio of the equation. The **limiting reagent** is the reactant that runs out first, and it determines how much product can form. The others are in **excess**. To identify it, compute the product each reactant could give, and the smallest amount wins. Equivalently, divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient: the smallest quotient marks the limiting reagent.

The **theoretical yield** is the maximum product, calculated from the limiting reagent. The **actual yield** is the amount obtained. Real yields are lower because of incomplete reaction, side reactions and losses during isolation.

example.title: Limiting reagent and percent yield
example.problem: 50.0 g of N₂ and 10.0 g of H₂ react by N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. (a) Which is limiting? (b) What is the theoretical yield of NH₃? (c) If 41.2 g is obtained, what is the percent yield?
solution: (a) n(N₂) = 50.0/28.01 = 1.785 mol; n(H₂) = 10.0/2.016 = 4.960 mol. Divide by coefficients: N₂ 1.785/1 = 1.785; H₂ 4.960/3 = 1.653. H₂ is smaller, so **H₂ is limiting**.

check.q: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. A mixture contains 2.0 mol Al and 2.0 mol Cl₂. Which is limiting?
check.why: Cl₂ gives 2.0/3 = 0.67 reaction units; Al gives 2.0/2 = 1.0.

check.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 8.00 g and an actual yield of 6.20 g. What is the percent yield?

sections.title: Concentration of solutions
body: A solution consists of a **solute** dissolved in a **solvent**. Its **concentration** is the amount of solute in a given amount of solution or solvent. Several measures are in use:

head: Measure
Definition
Units
Temperature-dependent?
rows: moles of solute / liters of solution
moles of solute / kilograms of solvent
mass of solute per 10⁶ (10⁹) mass of solution
table.caption: Concentration measures.

body: **Molarity** is the standard in the laboratory because volumes are easy to measure. Molality and mole fraction are used in thermodynamics and colligative properties, because they do not change as the solution expands on warming. For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 ppm is about 1 mg per liter.

example.title: Preparing a solution
example.problem: How many grams of NaCl are needed to prepare 250.0 mL of 0.100 M solution?
solution: Weigh the salt, dissolve it in less than 250 mL of water in a volumetric flask, then fill to the mark.

body: Adding solvent does not change the moles of solute, so for a **stock solution** diluted to a new concentration, n = M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

example.title: Dilution
example.problem: How much 12.0 M HCl is needed to make 500.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl?
solution: Add the acid to water, not water to acid, because the dilution is exothermic.

example.title: Molality and mole fraction
example.problem: 10.0 g of NaOH is dissolved in 250.0 g of water. Find the molality and the mole fraction of NaOH.

check.q: What is the molarity of a solution of 5.85 g NaCl in 500.0 mL?
A 100.0 mL sample of 2.00 M KNO₃ is diluted to 400.0 mL. What is the new concentration?

sections.title: Solution stoichiometry and titration
body: Reactions in solution are handled like those of pure substances, with moles found from n = MV. A **titration** applies this to measure an unknown. A solution of known concentration, the **titrant**, is added from a buret to a measured volume of the **analyte** until the reaction is exactly complete: the **equivalence point**, where the moles of titrant equal the moles required by the stoichiometry. An **indicator**, a dye that changes color near that point, signals the **end point**. A **standard solution** has an accurately known concentration, prepared from a pure, stable, weighable **primary standard**, such as potassium hydrogen phthalate for bases.

example.title: Acid–base titration
example.problem: A 25.00 mL sample of HCl is neutralized by 31.42 mL of 0.1000 M NaOH. Find the HCl concentration.
solution: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O: one mole of acid per mole of base.

example.title: Titration with a 1:2 ratio
example.problem: A 20.00 mL sample of H₂SO₄ requires 28.40 mL of 0.1500 M NaOH. Find [H₂SO₄].
solution: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. n(NaOH) = 0.1500 × 0.02840 = 4.260 × 10⁻³ mol, so n(H₂SO₄) = 2.130 × 10⁻³ mol.

body: The shape of titration curves, and why the equivalence point of a weak acid is not at pH 7, is treated in the chapter on acids and bases.

check.q: What is the equivalence point of a titration?
check.a: The point where moles of titrant exactly match the moles required by the reaction
wrong: The point where the indicator is added
Where the solution is neutral at pH 7
The point where the titrant runs out of the buret

check.q: How many mL of 0.100 M NaOH neutralize 20.0 mL of 0.150 M HCl?

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of O₂ when C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is balanced with the smallest whole numbers?
quiz.why: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O. The fractional coefficient 7/2 for one mole of ethane must be doubled to clear the fraction.

quiz.q: Which quantity is not necessarily the same on both sides of a balanced equation?
quiz.a: The total number of moles of molecules
wrong: The number of atoms of each element
quiz.why: Atoms, mass and charge are conserved. Molecules are not: in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, three moles of reactant molecules give two moles of product.

quiz.q: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, what mass of O₂ reacts completely with 4.00 g of H₂?
quiz.why: n(H₂) = 4.00/2.016 = 1.98 mol, the mole ratio O₂ : H₂ is 1 : 2, so n(O₂) = 0.992 mol, or 31.7 g. A 1 : 1 mole ratio would give 63.5 g.

quiz.q: What is the mass percent of nitrogen in (NH₄)₂SO₄ (M = 132.14 g/mol; N = 14.01)?
quiz.why: The formula has two N atoms: 2(14.01)/132.14 = 0.212. Counting one N gives 10.6%.

quiz.q: A hydrocarbon sample contains 4.80 g of carbon and 1.20 g of hydrogen. What is its empirical formula?
quiz.why: n(C) = 4.80/12.01 = 0.400 mol and n(H) = 1.20/1.008 = 1.19 mol, a ratio of 1 : 3. The empirical formula is the simplest ratio, so C₂H₆ is a molecular formula, not the answer.

quiz.q: Dividing mole amounts by the smallest gives the ratio 1 : 1.5 : 2 for three elements. What is the next step?
quiz.a: Multiply all three by 2 to get 2 : 3 : 4
wrong: Divide all three by 1.5 to make the middle number 1
Conclude that no compound with this composition exists
quiz.why: Ratios near a simple fraction such as 1.5 are scaled by the small integer that makes every number whole. Rounding 1.5 changes the formula.

quiz.q: Burning 1.000 g of a hydrocarbon gives 1.466 g of CO₂. How many grams of carbon did the sample contain?
quiz.why: n(C) = 1.466/44.01 = 0.03331 mol, and 0.03331 × 12.01 = 0.400 g. The 1.07 g is the oxygen in the CO₂, much of which came from the O₂ supply.

quiz.q: A mixture of 4.60 g Na and 3.55 g Cl₂ reacts by 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. What is the maximum mass of NaCl?
quiz.why: n(Na) = 0.200 mol needs 0.100 mol Cl₂, but only 0.0501 mol is present, so Cl₂ is limiting. NaCl = 2 × 0.0501 = 0.100 mol = 5.85 g. Adding the reactant masses (8.15 g) ignores the limit.

quiz.q: A reaction gives 9.00 g of product, which is a 72.0% yield. What was the theoretical yield?
quiz.why: Percent yield = actual/theoretical × 100%, so theoretical = 9.00/0.720 = 12.5 g. Multiplying by 0.720 would give an impossible value below the actual yield.

quiz.q: Which statement about limiting reagents is false?
quiz.a: The limiting reagent is the reactant present in the smallest mass
wrong: The limiting reagent determines the theoretical yield
Some of the excess reagent remains after the reaction is complete
Dividing each reactant's moles by its coefficient identifies the limiting reagent
quiz.why: Masses of different substances cannot be compared, since the reaction runs on moles and the equation's ratio. A small mass of a light reactant can be a large number of moles.

quiz.q: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 25.0 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (180.16 g/mol), in water to give 500.0 mL?
quiz.why: n = 25.0/180.16 = 0.139 mol, and M = 0.139 mol/0.5000 L = 0.278 M. The value 0.139 is the number of moles with the volume forgotten.

quiz.q: How much 6.00 M HNO₃ is needed to prepare 250.0 mL of 0.300 M HNO₃?
quiz.why: V₁ = M₂V₂/M₁ = (0.300)(250.0)/6.00 = 12.5 mL. The 238 mL figure is the water to add, and 5.00 × 10³ mL inverts the ratio.

quiz.q: A solution is warmed and expands slightly. Which concentration measure decreases?
quiz.why: Molarity divides by the volume of solution, which grows when it expands. The other three depend only on masses or moles, which do not change on warming.

quiz.q: A solution contains 11.7 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) in 400.0 g of water. What is its molality?
quiz.why: n(NaCl) = 0.200 mol and the solvent is 0.4000 kg, so m = 0.500 mol/kg. The value 0.200 is the number of moles, and 8.94 × 10⁻³ is the mole fraction.

quiz.q: A 2.5 L water sample contains 5.0 mg of dissolved lead. What is the concentration in ppm, taking 1 L of water as 1 kg?
quiz.why: For dilute aqueous solutions 1 ppm is 1 mg per liter (per kilogram), so 5.0 mg/2.5 L = 2.0 ppm.

quiz.q: A 20.00 mL sample of Ba(OH)₂ is neutralized by 25.00 mL of 0.1000 M HCl: Ba(OH)₂ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + 2H₂O. What is the molarity of the Ba(OH)₂?
quiz.why: n(HCl) = 2.500 × 10⁻³ mol, so n(Ba(OH)₂) = 1.250 × 10⁻³ mol, and the concentration is 1.250 × 10⁻³/0.02000 L = 0.0625 M. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 0.125 M.

quiz.q: Why is potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) used to standardize a NaOH solution?
quiz.a: It is a pure, stable solid that can be weighed accurately
wrong: It changes color at the equivalence point with NaOH
It is a stronger acid than HCl, so it reacts more completely
It reacts with NaOH in a 2 : 1 ratio, which reduces the error
quiz.why: A primary standard must be pure and stable so that its mass gives an accurately known number of moles. The color change comes from an indicator, which is a separate substance.

quiz.q: In a titration, the indicator changes color when 24.90 mL of titrant has been added, while the reaction is complete at 24.85 mL. The color change marks the
quiz.a: end point, which is close to but not the same as the equivalence point
wrong: equivalence point, since the indicator signals when the reaction is complete
primary standard, which is the point where titrant and analyte are equal
equivalence point, and the 0.05 mL is the experimental error in the burette
quiz.why: The equivalence point is defined by stoichiometry, the end point by the indicator's color change. A good indicator is chosen so that the two are very close.

summary: Balanced equations conserve atoms. Coefficients give mole ratios, never mass ratios.
Empirical formulas come from mole ratios of the elements. Multiply by an integer to match the molar mass.
Stoichiometry follows mass → mol → mol → mass. The limiting reagent sets the theoretical yield.
Molarity is moles per liter of solution. Molality, mole fraction and mass percent do not depend on temperature. For a dilution, M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
A titration finds an unknown concentration. At the equivalence point the moles of titrant match the stoichiometric requirement.

problems.q: Balance: (a) Al + HCl → AlCl₃ + H₂; (b) C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O; (c) KMnO₄ + HCl → KCl + MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + H₂O.
Vitamin C is 40.92% C, 4.58% H and 54.50% O by mass. Its molar mass is 176.1 g/mol. Find the empirical and molecular formulas.
problems.solution: In 100 g: C 3.407 mol, H 4.544 mol, O 3.406 mol. Dividing by 3.406: 1 : 1.334 : 1. Multiply by 3: C₃H₄O₃ (88.06 g/mol). 176.1/88.06 = 2.

problems.q: Iron is made by Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. 1.00 kg of Fe₂O₃ reacts with 0.600 kg of CO. Find the limiting reagent and the maximum mass of Fe.
problems.a: Fe₂O₃ is limiting; 699 g of Fe.

problems.q: Concentrated sulfuric acid is 98.0% H₂SO₄ by mass with density 1.84 g/mL. Find its molarity.
problems.solution: In 1 L: mass of solution 1840 g, of which 0.980 × 1840 = 1803 g is H₂SO₄. n = 1803/98.08 = 18.4 mol.

problems.q: A 0.5000 g sample of an impure Na₂CO₃ is titrated with 0.1000 M HCl; 42.50 mL is needed to reach the second equivalence point (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂). Find the mass percent of Na₂CO₃.
